intro: Two models can make identical class decisions while assigning very different probabilities. Evaluate the probabilities themselves.
task: Return the binary Brier score: the mean squared difference between predicted class-one probabilities and binary outcomes.
requirements: labels and probabilities are nonempty same-length finite vectors. Labels contain only zero and one.
Probabilities are in [0,1], including both endpoints.
Return mean((probabilities - labels)**2), with no square root, extra factor, or thresholding. Smaller is better.
Do not modify inputs. Raise ValueError for the invalid shapes, ranges, or non-finite numeric inputs described above. Numerical checks use moderate finite values unless stated otherwise.

hints.title: Choose the representation
hints.body: Subtract labels from probabilities before squaring elementwise.

hints.title: Check the boundary
hints.body: Do not convert probabilities into class predictions; that removes the confidence information.

explanation: The Brier score measures squared error of probability forecasts. A confident wrong forecast receives a larger penalty than an uncertain wrong forecast.
This binary convention uses a single probability for class one. It is not the sum of squared errors over two one-hot class columns, which would double the result.
Compare forecasts of 0.51 and 0.99 when the outcome is zero. Both cross a 0.5 decision threshold, but their losses differ. Explain what that adds beyond accuracy.
